summary: Light steel fire tower of the Tweed Fire District, built with the district's 1922 towers; no source found describes the site today.

facts.design: Light steel tower with an octagonal cupola; 80 ft tall per a fan site

events.note: Fan-site district notes say towers of the Tweed Fire District, including Mt. St. Patrick, were built in 1922; no separate date for this tower

evidence.supports: first observer James Guiney used pulleys and weights to avoid the climb
evidence.quote: The first observer was James Guiney, who apparently devised a system of pulleys and weights to ascend and descend the tower in order to avoid the long climb up the ladder.

evidence.supports: a weight dislodged, Guiney descended too fast, then resumed climbing the ladder
evidence.quote: One day one of the weights dislodged resulting in Guiney making a much more rapid descent than he wanted, after which he abandoned his apparatus and resumed climbing the ladder!

notes_for_editor: Location conflict to check before any site advice: firelookout.ca gives the address as Tweed, ON, but its published coordinates (45.30889, -76.89056) are about 98 km northeast of Tweed (my calculation, using Tweed at roughly 44.48 N, 77.32 W, which no source cited here gives). The Tweed label may be the fire district rather than the site, and the sources do not explain it. The brief has no local_unit for this record, and no source read names a local government unit, so the story gives no district beyond Tweed Fire District. Build year 1922 rests on a fan-site district list that gives the year for the group of towers rather than for this one. Mount St. Patrick is absent from the fan site's still-standing list, but that list is undated apart from a 2013 reference, so it is weak evidence of its fate. The full page was searched on 2026-10-20 and has no St. Patrick entry. The 1940s transfer of some Tweed towers to the Lindsay District is in the fan site's notes but does not name St. Patrick, so it is left out. No source read describes the site today. The Ontario GeoHub tower layer (data/raw/ontario_lio/fire_towers.geojson) has no point with this name near these coordinates (the nearest listed tower is roughly 88 km away by a rough calculation), so it was not used. A yolasite Southern Ontario fire tower map (search snippet only, page returns 403) also lists it in the Tweed district. Possible follow-up: the 1977 Pembroke topographic map sheet (not read), Forest History Ontario, or Hastings and Renfrew newspapers for fate.
